messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 37, Daniel had spent most of his adult life in work that rewarded precision and control. As a database administrator, he was used to long hours in a cool server room and the reassuring logic of systems that could be monitored, corrected, and backed up. His illness shattered that sense of order. What began as a period of unexplained breathing difficulty ended in an emergency hospitalization when he became acutely short of breath and was rushed through a cascade of tests, oxygen, IV lines, and repeated examinations. He still described the worst moments less in terms of pain than of helplessness: lying flat, watching staff move quickly around him, seeing needles and tubing approach, and feeling that each breath might be the one that failed. The terror of that time seemed bound to the sensory details of it. Even now, anything that echoed those moments—tightness in his chest, the sensation of not getting a full breath, a blood draw tray, a hospital corridor—could pull him back into the same fear.

In the months after he recovered medically, Daniel did not feel recovered in any ordinary sense. He was carrying around strong, difficult emotions that came on with startling force: fear first, but also anger at his body and a quiet shame about how panicked he had been. He said his body no longer felt neutral to him; it felt primed, tight, watchful, as if danger could break through at any moment. When something reminded him of the hospitalization, his reaction was immediate and physical. His chest tightened, his heart raced, and he felt a jolt of alarm that made him brace himself before he had fully registered what had set it off. It was out of this constant sense of threat that his habits began to change. He became determined to manage anything that might stir up bodily sensations or place him back in contact with medical settings.

Daniel started by avoiding exercise. Before the illness he had occasionally used the treadmill in his apartment gym, but he gave it up completely because any increase in breathing felt too close to the start of the medical crisis. He also began eating in a rigid, controlling way, restricting what and when he ate because the discipline itself made him feel less vulnerable, more able to keep his body from doing something unpredictable. Most noticeably, he avoided medical cues wherever he could. He postponed routine checkups, looked away from clinic advertisements, and took a longer route to his office building if an ambulance was parked near the hospital entrance across the street. These strategies made sense to him in the moment, because they seemed to lower the chance that he would feel that old terror again, but they also kept his world narrowed around the possibility of danger. The less he tested his body and the less contact he had with ordinary medical situations, the more tense and reactive he became.

That pattern had tightened over time. Because he avoided exercise, ordinary exertion left him deconditioned, and climbing the stairs at work could bring on mild breathlessness that felt immediately ominous. Because he restricted eating so strictly, physical sensations in his body became something he monitored closely and mistrusted. Because he steered clear of examinations and hospitals, the sight of medical equipment remained charged and unfamiliar rather than ordinary. In his daily work life this was increasingly hard to hide. When a coworker mentioned a recent outpatient procedure, Daniel felt his shoulders lock and had to leave the break room. During a workplace health screening, the glimpse of needles on a supply cart brought on such a strong physical reaction that he told his manager he was ill and went home. Even seeing a drip stand on a television show in the office lounge could leave him keyed up for hours.

These same strategies also made the threat feel more convincing to him. Each time he skipped a physical exam, he was briefly relieved, but he was also more certain afterward that he could not handle one. Each time he avoided exertion, he had less confidence in his breathing. Each time he controlled his eating more tightly, he felt more preoccupied with his body and more easily frightened by it. Daniel had come to believe that if he let his guard down—even with something as simple as jogging, a checkup, or sitting through a blood draw—he might be overwhelmed again, trapped in the same horror and helplessness he felt in the hospital.

By the time he sought help, the problem had spread well beyond the original illness. He was divorced and living alone, and he had become increasingly isolated, telling himself he was just being careful. What finally brought him in was a recent episode at work: after hurrying across the parking lot and arriving short of breath, he felt a surge of panic so intense that he had to lock himself in a restroom stall until the shaking passed. He was frightened by how quickly his body could still turn on him, and by how small his life had become around avoiding that fear. More than anything, Daniel wanted to stop living as if the next breath might be a threat.
